The model predicted the system recharge and discharge capacities, total power demand, and TES water temperatures very well. Deviations occurred in predicting the compressor discharge temperatures and pressures in this test, starting during the second discharge / end of the first recharge operation when subcooled refrigerant Page 88 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park accumulated at the outlet of the BPHX and before the EXV. This subcooled refrigerant did not have sufficient time to redistribute in the HP-TES cycle during mode switching, resulting in significantly higher compressor discharge pressures. Despite this deviation, the observed model discharge pressures and temperatures in this validation matched those of Test 8H (Figure 69), indicating model validity. The design considerations and associated justifications are shown in Table 20, leveraging lessons learned from laboratory testing conducted at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Table 20: Hydronic loop design considerations and justifications Consideration Justification Page 89 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park Air release valves • Removing air pockets to minimize hydronic loop pressure included drop, learned from ORNL shakedown tests 1.25-inch pipe internal • Minimize piping pressure drops & pumping power diameter • 20% safety factor considering brazed PHX, TES units, piping, & fittings Pump considerations: • ORNL experimental data used for PHX and TES unit 90-ft head pressure drops • EPRI field measurements used piping distances Preserve plant life & • Decrease spending on building and plant life restoration building aesthetic after testing Flow control valves & flow • Ensure equal hydronic fluid flow rates in each TES tank meters on each TES tank Environmental Concerns • Ensure no PCM and/or Glycol leaks in the field test Secondary loop • Pressure, temperature, & flow meter locations considered instrumentation for model validation purposes The drawings for the field unit hydronic loop are shown in Figure 87, which was finalized following a thorough site walkthrough. Based on available space and weight limitations, the hydronic loop pumping station was placed on the roof, and the two thermal batteries were installed at ground level. The pump was sized to meet a pressure head of 90 ft, considering an internal piping diameter of 1.25 inches. The air release valves were installed at the highest point of the hydronic loop to allow air bubbles to be removed during commissioning. The secondary loop sensors were installed as close as possible to the component ports to minimize deviations caused by piping heating gains or pressure losses, for model validation purposes.
